You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose exactly 1 design.
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: $v_{out\_min} \ge 1.8\text{V}$, $v_{out\_max} \le 3.6\text{V}$, ripple $\le 0.05\text{V}$, $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$, settled $\le 0.02\text{V}$.
    *   Piezo: Sinusoidal current source $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p=25\text{nF}$ and $20\text{M}\Omega$ leakage.
    *   Open-circuit voltage amplitude: $\sim 3.2\text{V}$ (very low, so diode drops are critical).
    *   Previous design ('Parallel-SSHI-Bridge'): A full-bridge rectifier combined with an L-S switch (attempting some sort of SSHI/synchronous extraction).
    *   Previous results: Failed most conditions. $v_{avg}$ was too low (around $0.9\text{V}$ for S1).
    *   The "screening" result for 'Parallel-SSHI-Bridge' was actually good (it delivered $>100\%$ of required power), but the simulation failed. This implies the topology *can* deliver power, but the way it's configured (or the values) is preventing it from reaching the target $1.8\text{V}$ in a real cold-start simulation.

    *   Looking at 'Parallel-SSHI-Bridge':
        *   D1-D4: Full bridge (pzp->out, pzn->out, 0->pzp, 0->pzn).
        *   L1 and S1: L1 is between pzp and n1, S1 is between n1 and pzn.
        *   This is a parallel L-S branch. When S1 closes, L1 is connected across pzp and pzn.
        *   The problem: L1-S1 is in parallel with the piezo. This doesn't shift the voltage in the way a series SSHI does. It might act as a resonant energy extractor, but it's not boosting the voltage effectively.
        *   Since the open-circuit voltage is very low ($3.2\text{V}$ peak), a standard full-bridge (FBR) loses $2 \times 0.25\text{V} = 0.5\text{V}$ to diode drops. FBR reached $2.24\text{V}$ for S1. The Parallel-SSHI-Bridge performed *worse* than the FBR.

    *   Low voltage source $\rightarrow$ diode drops are the enemy.
    *   Standard FBR: $V_{out} \approx V_{piezo\_peak} - 2 V_f$.
    *   To improve $V_{out}$, we need a way to "flip" the charge on $C_p$ (SSHI - Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) or use a charge pump/boost.
    *   Standard SSHI uses a switch and inductor to invert the voltage on $C_p$ at the peaks.
    *   Let's try a basic SSHI topology.
    *   Basic SSHI:
        *   Piezo $\rightarrow$ Rectifier $\rightarrow$ Storage Capacitor.
        *   Switch and Inductor are used to flip $C_p$'s voltage.
        *   Wait, the prompt says the piezo is a current source $I_p \sin(\omega t)$ in parallel with $C_p$.
        *   The voltage across the piezo is $V_{pzp} - V_{pzn}$.
        *   To implement SSHI, we need to short the piezo with an inductor $L$ at the peaks of the voltage.

    *   Let's reconsider the circuit. The most efficient way to extract energy from a low-voltage piezo is to use an inductor to invert the voltage on $C_p$ when the current source has pushed $C_p$ to its maximum voltage.
    *   SSHI structure:
        1.  Rectifier: A half-bridge (or full-bridge) to charge $C_{out}$.
        2.  Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$: Connected across the piezo terminals (pzp and pzn) to flip the voltage.
        3.  Sync: Closes $S$ at the voltage extrema.

    *   Wait, if I use a full bridge rectifier, I have:
        *   D1: pzp $\rightarrow$ out
        *   D2: pzn $\rightarrow$ out (Wait, that's not a full bridge. A full bridge is pzp->out, pzn->out, 0->pzp, 0->pzn? No, that's wrong.)
        *   Correct Full Bridge:
            *   D1: pzp $\rightarrow$ out
            *   D2: pzn $\rightarrow$ out (No)
            *   A full bridge should be:
                *   Rectifier part: pzp $\rightarrow$ out (D1), pzn $\rightarrow$ out (D2)? No.
                *   Let's use the reference FBR: `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`.
                *   Let's trace that:
                    *   pzp positive: Current flows pzp $\rightarrow$ out $\rightarrow$ RL $\rightarrow$ 0 $\rightarrow$ pzn (via D4).
                    *   pzn positive: Current flows pzn $\rightarrow$ out $\rightarrow$ RL $\rightarrow$ 0 $\rightarrow$ pzp (via D3).
                    *   This is indeed a full bridge.

    *   Now, add the SSHI part:
        *   An inductor $L$ and switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo terminals (pzp and pzn).
        *   $S$ closes at the peaks of $V_{piezo}$.
        *   This flips the charge on $C_p$, increasing the voltage available to the rectifier.

    *   Let's refine the SSHI:
        *   Components:
            *   D1: pzp $\rightarrow$ out (DSCH)
            *   D2: pzn $\rightarrow$ out (DSCH)
            *   D3: 0 $\rightarrow$ pzp (DSCH)
            *   D4: 0 $\rightarrow$ pzn (DSCH)
            *   L1: pzp $\rightarrow$ n1
            *   S1: n1 $\rightarrow$ pzn (ctrl=G1)
            *   G1: SYNC (ton, phase, edges=both)
            *   C1: out $\rightarrow$ 0
            *   DZ1: 0 $\rightarrow$ out (DZ33) to clamp at 3.3 V.

    *   Wait, the previous design 'Parallel-SSHI-Bridge' was *exactly* this. Why did it fail?
        *   Design 1: `D1 pzp out, D2 pzn out, D3 0 pzp, D4 0 pzn, L1 pzp n1, S1 n1 pzn, G1 SYNC, C1 out 0, DZ1 0 out`.
        *   Wait, that is the same topology. Why did it perform worse than FBR?
        *   FBR (no L-S) reached $2.24\text{V}$.
        *   Parallel-SSHI-Bridge reached $0.93\text{V}$.
        *   This is strange. If the SSHI is correctly timed, it should *increase* the voltage. If it's poorly timed, it could potentially sink energy or just act as a load.
        *   Maybe the `ton` or `phase` was wrong? But the prompt says values are optimized automatically.
        *   Actually, look at the FBR again: $V_{out}$ was $2.24\text{V}$ (S1). $V_{out\_min}$ is $1.8\text{V}$.
        *   FBR failed "settled" and "S2" (heavy load).
        *   S2 heavy load: $V_{avg} = 1.76\text{V}$ (needs $1.8\text{V}$).
        *   S3 strong excitation: $V_{avg} = 5.68\text{V}$ (needs $\le 3.6\text{V}$).
        *   S4 weak excitation: $V_{avg} = 1.51\text{V}$ (needs $1.8\text{V}$).

    *   So FBR is close! We just need a bit more boost for S2 and S4, and a way to clamp S3.
    *   The Zener diode (DZ33) can clamp S3.
    *   To boost S2 and S4, we need SSHI to actually work.

    *   Why did the previous SSHI fail?
        *   Maybe the inductor was too large or the switch was interfering?
        *   Actually, in a standard SSHI, the inductor and switch are usually used to invert the voltage *before* the rectifier.
        *   Wait, if we have a full bridge, the piezo terminals are pzp and pzn. The inductor and switch are in parallel with pzp and pzn. This *is* the standard SSHI.
        *   Let's try a different approach to the rectifier. A half-bridge rectifier is more efficient (one diode drop instead of two).
        *   Half-bridge:
            *   pzn connected to 0.
            *   D1: pzp $\rightarrow$ out.
            *   But the piezo is a current source in parallel with $C_p$ *between* pzp and pzn. If we tie pzn to 0, we only get half the cycle.
            *   Unless we use the inductor to flip the voltage, and *then* use a half-bridge.
            *   Wait, if we flip the voltage every half cycle using $L$ and $S$, we can use a single diode to harvest everything.
            *   SSHI Half-Bridge:
                1.  D1: pzp $\rightarrow$ out.
                2.  S1: pzp $\rightarrow$ pzn (via L1).
                3.  G1: SYNC (edges=both).
                4.  C1: out $\rightarrow$ 0.
                5.  This is the "Parallel-SSHI" but with a half-bridge.

    *   Wait, let's look at the "Reference Design: FBR". It used 4 diodes and 2.2 uF.
        *   S2 (150k load) gave $1.76\text{V}$.
        *   S4 (1M load, 30uA Ip) gave $1.51\text{V}$.
        *   These are very close to $1.8\text{V}$.
        *   The most critical issue is the diode drop. If we can reduce the drop from $2 \times 0.25\text{V}$ to $1 \times 0.25\text{V}$, we gain $0.25\text{V}$.
        *   $1.76\text{V} + 0.25\text{V} = 2.01\text{V}$ (S2 OK).
        *   $1.51\text{V} + 0.25\text{V} = 1.76\text{V}$ (S4 almost OK).

    *   How to get a one-diode drop?
        *   Connect pzn to 0.
        *   Now the piezo is between pzp and 0.
        *   Current is $I_p \sin(\omega t)$.
        *   The voltage is $V_p \sin(\omega t)$.
        *   We can't use a half-bridge without the SSHI flip because we'd only get the positive half-cycle.
        *   But if we use the SSHI flip at both peaks (edges=both), we can keep the voltage at pzp always positive.
        *   Actually, the lapped-transformer or some other SSHI versions exist, but let's stick to the basics.

    *   Let's try the SSHI with a half-bridge:
        *   D1: pzp $\rightarrow$ out (DSCH)
        *   L1: pzp $\rightarrow$ n1
        *   S1: n1 $\rightarrow$ pzn (ctrl=G1)
        *   G1: SYNC (edges=both, ton=..., phase=...)
        *   C1: out $\rightarrow$ 0
        *   DZ1: 0 $\rightarrow$ out (DZ33)
        *   Wait, this requires pzn to be 0? No, the SYNC closes S1 to connect pzp to pzn via L1.
        *   If we use a half-bridge, we need a return path for the current.
        *   Let's try:
            *   D1: pzp $\rightarrow$ out
            *   L1: pzp $\rightarrow$ n1
            *   S1: n1 $\rightarrow$ pzn
            *   G1: SYNC
            *   L2: pzn $\rightarrow$ 0? No.
            *   Wait, if we just tie pzn to 0, we have:
                *   D1: pzp $\rightarrow$ out
                *   L1: pzp $\rightarrow$ n1
                *   S1: n1 $\rightarrow$ 0
                *   C1: out $\rightarrow$ 0
                *   This would flip the voltage on $C_p$ (which is now between pzp and 0).
                *   But is it allowed to tie pzn to 0? The piezo model is between pzp and pzn. Yes, that's just a connection.

    *   Let's try the "Half-Bridge SSHI":
        *   D1: pzp $\rightarrow$ out (DSCH)
        *   L1: pzp $\rightarrow$ n1
        *   S1: n1 $\rightarrow$ pzn (ctrl=G1)
        *   S2: pzn $\rightarrow$ 0 (Wait, we can't just use a switch. Let's just use a resistor of 1 Ohm or just connect pzn to 0).
        *   Correction: Just connect pzn to 0 using a resistor (though the rules say nodes must have 2 connections).
        *   Let's just connect pzn to 0 with a very low value resistor (e.g., $1\Omega$). Or better, use the FBR structure but optimize it.

    *   Wait! I have a better idea. What if we use a "Synchronous Rectifier"?
        *   The prompt allows SYNC switches.
        *   Instead of diodes, use switches to rectify.
        *   S1: pzp $\rightarrow$ out
        *   S2: pzn $\rightarrow$ out
        *   S3: 0 $\rightarrow$ pzp
        *   S4: 0 $\rightarrow$ pzn
        *   But we only have 4 switches total.
        *   And a SYNC only works at the extrema. Rectification requires switches to be closed for the *entire* half-cycle.
        *   The SYNC controller described here is specifically for "ton" pulses at the extrema. It is *not* a general-purpose PWM or phase-locked rectifier. It's for SSHI.

    *   Let's go back to the FBR. Why did it fail "settled" and "S3"?
        *   S3: $V_{avg} = 5.68\text{V}$ (too high, max 3.6V).
        *   S1, S5: "settled" failed. This means $|mean(0.7-0.8) - mean(0.6-0.7)| > 0.02\text{V}$.
        *   This happens if the storage capacitor is too large, so it's still charging at 0.8s.
        *   FBR used $C = 2.2\mu\text{F}$.
        *   Let's check the time constant. For S1: $RL = 330\text{k}\Omega$, $C = 2.2\mu\text{F}$. $\tau = RC = 330\text{k} \times 2.2\mu = 0.726\text{s}$.
        *   With $\tau = 0.7\text{s}$, the voltage will definitely still be drifting at $t=0.8\text{s}$.
        *   To pass "settled", we need a smaller $C_{out}$.
        *   But if $C_{out}$ is too small, "ripple" ($v_{pp}$) will increase.
